steps.text: Apply downward pressure through the armpit onto uke's elbow joint. Combined with the wrist pull, this hyperextends the elbow.

steps.title: Maintain position and apply consistent pressure
steps.text: Hold the lock firmly. In standing application, apply enough pressure to force a submission or take uke down. In ne-waza, increase pressure until submission.

principles: The arm must be fully straightened. Any bend in the elbow means no hyperextension pressure exists.
The armpit clamp must be over the upper arm just proximal to the elbow — too far up the arm is ineffective.
Waki-Gatame has standing application — it can be applied during grip fighting when tori controls uke's arm and has an opportunity to clamp.
Control of the wrist and the armpit pressure must work together — losing wrist control allows uke to bend the elbow and escape.

mistakes.mistake: Elbow not fully extended before clamping
mistakes.fix: Pull the arm straight before clamping. If the elbow is bent, re-straighten it by pulling the wrist or sleeve.

mistakes.mistake: Armpit positioned on the shoulder instead of upper arm
mistakes.fix: The clamp should be on the upper arm, just above the elbow. Clamping on the shoulder has no joint-lock leverage.

mistakes.mistake: Not controlling the wrist
mistakes.fix: Secure the wrist at all times. A free wrist allows uke to rotate their arm or bend the elbow to escape.

mistakes.mistake: In standing application — leaning too far forward
mistakes.fix: Maintain your own balance while applying the lock. Leaning excessively forward makes you vulnerable to being thrown.

when_to_use: Waki-Gatame is applied opportunistically — when uke's arm is straight and accessible for the armpit clamp. In standing, it arises during grip fighting when tori can trap the arm. In ne-waza, it appears in scrambles and transitions when the elbow presents. It is one of the few kansetsu-waza with meaningful standing application. Note: in IJF competition, falling directly to the mat while applying a standing Waki-Gatame results in hansoku-make (disqualification).

faq.q: Can Waki-Gatame be applied standing?
faq.a: Yes — Waki-Gatame is one of the few kansetsu-waza with a meaningful standing application. During grip fighting, if tori gains control of uke's arm and can clamp the armpit, the lock can be applied to force a standing submission or a takedown.

faq.q: What is the risk of Waki-Gatame to uke?
faq.a: Waki-Gatame hyperextends the elbow joint. Applied with force or if uke does not tap in time, it can injure the elbow ligaments or hyperextend the joint. Both partners should practice with control and tap early.

name: Yama-Arashi
overview: Yama-Arashi is a powerful and technically demanding te-waza associated with the legendary judoka Saigo Shiro. Tori applies a high sleeve grip and a deep collar or sleeve grip, then executes a sweeping rotational throw that combines elements of Seoi-Nage and a large sweeping arm action — projecting uke with tremendous force in a storm-like arc. It is classified as te-waza but has characteristics of both shoulder throws and sweeping throws.

videos.title: This Is Technically Its Own Judo Throw - Yama Arashi
On the Mat with Sensei Jose: Yama Arashi, Forwards and Backwards

kuzushi.label: Off-balance
kuzushi.text: Kuzushi is created by a high, pulling action on uke's right sleeve — lifting uke's arm high and pulling them forward and to their right front corner. The lapel or second grip is used to drive uke's upper body into rotation. The high sleeve creates an off-balance that uke cannot easily counter by lowering their hips.

tsukuri.label: Entry
tsukuri.text: Step deeply in with the right foot, rotating to face the same direction as uke. The entry is similar to Seoi-Nage, but the left arm — gripping high on the sleeve or lapel — maintains an elevated, sweeping position rather than wrapping under the armpit. The body entry is tight against uke's chest.

kake.label: Execution
kake.text: Execute a powerful rotational movement — tori's body rotates forward while the high sleeve arm sweeps uke's right arm in a large downward arc. The combination of body rotation and the sweeping arm action creates a storm-like force that projects uke forward and over. The throw can be completed standing or with a partial drop.

steps.title: Establish a high sleeve grip
steps.text: Grip uke's right sleeve as high as possible — near the elbow or even the upper arm. This elevated grip is the key mechanical feature of Yama-Arashi.

steps.title: Create kuzushi with upward pull
steps.text: Pull uke's right arm upward and toward their right front corner. The high grip amplifies the destabilizing effect. Uke's right shoulder rises.

steps.title: Step in and turn
steps.text: Step the right foot in front of uke, between their feet, and pivot to face the same direction. Your back presses to uke's chest as in Seoi-Nage entry.

steps.title: Initiate the sweeping arm action
steps.text: With the high sleeve grip, begin a large downward sweeping arc — bringing uke's arm forward, down, and across. This creates the rotational storm force.

steps.title: Complete the rotational throw
steps.text: Your body rotates fully forward as the sweeping arm drives uke's upper body over. Uke is projected in a large arc to the mat.

principles: The high sleeve grip is the defining feature — without it, the throw becomes a standard Seoi-Nage. The elevation of the grip creates the unique sweeping arc.
The sweeping arm action must be large and continuous — like a storm sweeping through. Short, jerky pulls do not generate the necessary rotational force.
Body rotation and the arm sweep must be synchronized. Arm-only or body-only effort produces a weak, easily-countered throw.
Yama-Arashi requires exceptional timing and sensitivity — it is a high-level throw that should not be attempted without solid foundation in shoulder throw mechanics.

mistakes.mistake: Gripping at the wrist instead of high on the sleeve
mistakes.fix: The grip must be at the elbow or higher. A wrist grip lacks the leverage needed for the sweeping arc and limits the technique to a standard Seoi entry.

mistakes.mistake: Insufficient body rotation
mistakes.fix: The full body must rotate forward through the throw. Half-rotations leave uke on top of tori rather than projected forward.

mistakes.mistake: Treating Yama-Arashi as simply a strong Seoi-Nage
mistakes.fix: The sweeping arm arc is distinctive. Focus on the large circular motion of the sleeve arm rather than just a forward shoulder entry.

mistakes.mistake: Applying without sufficient kuzushi
mistakes.fix: Yama-Arashi requires uke's arm and shoulder to be elevated before entry. Attempting without the high kuzushi means uke can resist the entry.

when_to_use: Yama-Arashi is most effective against opponents with a stiff, upright posture where the high sleeve grip can be established. It is a specialized technique for practitioners who have mastered Seoi-Nage and shoulder throw mechanics and want to develop a high-power variation. In competition it is used as a surprise element against opponents who have defended standard Seoi-Nage entries.

faq.q: Who is Yama-Arashi historically associated with?
faq.a: Yama-Arashi is traditionally associated with Saigo Shiro, one of Jigoro Kano's most celebrated early students, who was said to have used it with devastating effect. His story inspired the novel and film "Sugata Sanshiro."

faq.q: How does Yama-Arashi differ from Seoi-Nage?
faq.a: Yama-Arashi uses a high sleeve grip (near the elbow) and a large sweeping arm arc, whereas Seoi-Nage typically uses a sleeve grip at the cuff with the other arm entering under the armpit. The sweeping rotational dynamic of Yama-Arashi is its defining characteristic.

name: Yoko-Gake
overview: Yoko-Gake is a side sacrifice throw in which tori steps across uke's front, hooks their foot against uke's near ankle, and falls to the side to sweep uke's foot and drop them laterally. Unlike rear sacrifice throws where tori falls backward, in Yoko-Gake tori falls directly to the side. The foot hook and side fall combine to take both tori and uke down together, with uke landing on the mat beside or slightly ahead of tori. It is a versatile technique that can be applied from various angles.

videos.title: Neil Adams spots a trend on the WJT: Yoko Gake
How To Yoko Gake || Competition Variation
Nage-no-kata: Yoko-Gake Tips | Riki Judo Dojo

kuzushi.label: Off-balance
kuzushi.text: Pull uke's sleeve arm sharply to your right and slightly downward, breaking their balance to their right front corner. The lapel arm lifts and draws uke's upper body forward and to your right. Uke's weight shifts onto their right foot in preparation for their right foot to be hooked.

tsukuri.label: Entry
tsukuri.text: Step your left foot to the outside of uke's right foot, crossing in front of uke. As you step, begin your sideward falling motion to the right. Hook your right foot against the outside of uke's right ankle — the hooking action places your right foot on the mat and sweeps uke's ankle inward.

kake.label: Execution
kake.text: Fall to your right side while simultaneously hooking uke's right ankle with your right foot in a lateral sweeping motion. Pull the sleeve arm sharply downward and to your right as you fall. The side fall with the ankle hook takes uke's right foot out from under them and uke falls laterally to land on the mat beside you.

steps.title: Break balance to uke's right front
steps.text: Pull the sleeve arm forward and to the right while the lapel arm draws uke's upper body toward you. Shift uke's weight onto their right foot.

steps.title: Step across uke's front
steps.text: Step your left foot to the outside of and in front of uke's right foot. You are now crossing in front of uke's body.

steps.title: Hook the ankle
steps.text: Hook your right foot against the outside of uke's right ankle. The hook is low and lateral — your foot sweeps uke's ankle inward.

steps.title: Initiate the side fall
steps.text: Commit to falling directly to your right side — not backward, not forward, directly sideward. Keep your body connected to uke.

steps.title: Complete with sleeve pull
steps.text: As you fall, pull the sleeve arm sharply downward and to your right, directing uke's fall laterally. Uke lands on the mat beside you.

principles: The fall must be directly to the side — a backward lean converts this to a poor sacrifice throw that puts tori in danger.
The ankle hook must be low and contact the outside of uke's ankle, not the shin or calf.
The sleeve arm pull is essential — without it, uke simply steps over your falling body.
The hook must be applied as uke's weight is shifting onto the right foot but before it is fully loaded — a fully planted, heavily weighted foot resists the lateral sweep.

mistakes.mistake: Falling backward instead of directly to the side
mistakes.fix: Yoko-Gake is a side sacrifice, not rear. Falling backward removes the ankle hook from uke's foot path and destroys the direction of the throw.

mistakes.mistake: Hooking too high on the shin instead of the ankle
mistakes.fix: The hook should contact uke's ankle. A shin hook has less leverage and is easier for uke to step over.

mistakes.mistake: Losing grip contact during the fall
mistakes.fix: Maintain firm grips on sleeve and lapel throughout the fall and throw. Releasing during the sacrifice leaves uke free to step over you.

mistakes.mistake: Attempting on an opponent moving toward you
mistakes.fix: Yoko-Gake works best when uke is stationary or moving to the side. Against an opponent advancing directly toward you, the step-across is difficult to time.

when_to_use: Yoko-Gake is effective against a stationary or laterally moving opponent. It works well from a circular movement pattern where uke's weight is momentarily on one foot. It is often used as a counter when uke resists a lateral pull, and as a complement to harai-goshi or de-ashi-barai combinations where lateral footwork is established.

faq.q: What distinguishes Yoko-Gake from other sacrifice throws?
faq.a: Yoko-Gake is a side sacrifice — tori falls directly to the side, not backward. This distinguishes it from rear sacrifice throws (ma-sutemi-waza) like Tomoe-Nage and Sumi-Gaeshi, and from other side sacrifices by its specific ankle hook and lateral fall direction.

faq.q: Does tori land beside uke in Yoko-Gake?
faq.a: Yes. Both tori and uke fall together — tori lands on their side and uke lands beside them. This is a characteristic of yoko-sutemi-waza (side sacrifice techniques).

faq.q: Is Yoko-Gake used in competition?
faq.a: Yes, particularly at intermediate competition levels. It is less common at elite levels, where opponents are more resistant to the lateral setup. However, it appears as a surprise technique and is effective in combinations.

name: Yoko-Guruma
overview: Yoko-Guruma is an advanced side sacrifice throw where tori dives under uke's arm or across uke's body, falling to the side and creating a wheel-like rotational throw. Tori's body acts as the axle around which uke is wheeled over in a large arc. It is one of the more spectacular throws in judo and requires significant practice to time correctly.

kuzushi.label: Off-balance
kuzushi.text: Kuzushi for Yoko-Guruma involves driving uke upward and to the side, opening space for tori to enter below uke's center of gravity. A high pulling action on the sleeve drives uke's arm upward while tori dives under it. The upward pull and the diving entry create the kuzushi by disturbing uke's upright equilibrium.

tsukuri.label: Entry
tsukuri.text: Tori dives or steps rapidly under uke's elevated arm, sliding their body across and below uke. One arm may wrap around uke's waist or thigh as tori slides through. The entry is low and across uke's body, setting up the side sacrifice position with uke above tori.

kake.label: Execution
kake.text: Fall to the side while pulling uke over with the grips and body contact. Tori's body rolling to the side creates the wheel motion that carries uke over in a large arc. Uke is wheeled sideways over tori's body and lands on the mat.

steps.title: Elevate uke's arm with sleeve grip
steps.text: Pull the sleeve arm high, elevating uke's arm to create space below it for tori's entry.

steps.title: Drive under uke's arm
steps.text: Rapidly dive under or across uke's elevated arm, sliding your body below uke's center of gravity.

steps.title: Wrap uke's waist or thigh
steps.text: As you slide under, wrap one arm around uke's waist or thigh to establish the contact point for the wheel.

steps.title: Fall to the side — the sacrifice
steps.text: Fall to the side decisively. Your body becomes the axle of the wheel.

steps.title: Wheel uke over
steps.text: Pull uke with grips and body as you fall, wheeling them over in a large arc. Uke lands on the mat beside or beyond tori.

principles: The entry under uke's arm must be fast and committed. Hesitating in the entry exposes tori to counters.
Body wrap at the waist or thigh creates the wheel axle. Without this contact point, tori falls away without the wheel mechanics.
The "wheel" effect comes from tori's side fall creating rotational force on uke. The fall direction must be perpendicular to uke's standing axis.
Yoko-Guruma is an advanced technique best drilled from specific setups or counters rather than as an arbitrary attack.

mistakes.mistake: Not diving deep enough — staying above uke's hip
mistakes.fix: The entry must get tori's body below uke's center of gravity. Staying at hip height or above gives uke leverage to counter.

mistakes.mistake: Falling backward instead of directly sideways
mistakes.fix: The sacrifice should be directly to the side to create the wheel motion. Falling backward creates a different (less effective) vector.

mistakes.mistake: No body wrap — losing contact with uke
mistakes.fix: Establish a wrap on uke's waist or thigh during the entry. Without contact, tori's fall is disconnected from uke and no throw occurs.

mistakes.mistake: Entry without elevated sleeve grip opening
mistakes.fix: Create the space under uke's arm first by elevating the sleeve. Diving into a closed arm position leaves no room for the entry.

when_to_use: Yoko-Guruma is used as an advanced counter when uke is pushing or pressing forward, or as a high-level attack from a grip fight. It is particularly striking when used as a counter to uke's forward throw attempts. The diving entry under the arm is a hallmark of advanced judo.

faq.q: What makes Yoko-Guruma an advanced technique?
faq.a: The diving entry under uke's elevated arm requires precise timing and body control. The technique demands a deep understanding of spacing, the correct sacrifice angle, and the coordination between the grips and the body roll.

faq.q: What does "guruma" mean in Yoko-Guruma?
faq.a: "Guruma" means wheel. In Yoko-Guruma, tori's body acts as the axle of a horizontal wheel, with uke being wheeled over sideways in a large arc.

name: Yoko-Otoshi
overview: Yoko-Otoshi is a side sacrifice throw in which tori steps across in front of uke's advancing leg or both legs, drops laterally to the side, and extends their own leg to block uke's shins or ankles while using an arm pull to topple uke sideways. The throw is from the classical Gokyo no Waza (originally placed in the second group). It differs from Tani-Otoshi in that the drop is to the side — perpendicular to uke's line of travel — rather than directly behind. The side drop mechanics mean tori falls perpendicular to uke while the blocking leg intercepts forward movement, creating a lateral topple.

videos.title: How and why Yoko-Otoshi works so well.
Yoko Otoshi | Side Sacrifice Throwing While Sliding

kuzushi.label: Off-balance
kuzushi.text: Pull uke forward and diagonally to the side — typically with the sleeve grip pulling across tori's front — to displace uke's weight laterally. As uke's weight shifts in that direction and their forward movement is already committed, the combination of lateral pull and forward shin block creates a kuzushi that is both sideways and rotational.

tsukuri.label: Entry
tsukuri.text: Step your lead foot across and in front of uke's advancing shin or ankle — positioning it as a lateral barrier. Drop your body to the side, extending your body perpendicular to uke. Your extended arm (sleeve grip) creates the blocking line along uke's advancing legs.

kake.label: Execution
kake.text: As you drop to the side, your extended leg (or arm along the mat) blocks uke's shin-level forward progress. The sleeve-grip pull topples uke's upper body sideways and forward over the blocking barrier. Uke falls to the side — perpendicular to their original direction of travel.

steps.title: Create forward movement in uke
steps.text: Use your grips to pull uke forward and toward the side you intend to throw. Uke must be stepping forward — Yoko-Otoshi requires forward momentum to exploit.

steps.title: Step across in front of uke's advancing leg
steps.text: Step your foot across and in front of uke's forward leg (or between uke's legs for a two-legged block). This step positions your leg as a lateral shin-level barrier.

steps.title: Drop to the side perpendicular to uke
steps.text: Drop your body to the same side as your blocking leg, falling perpendicular to uke's line of movement. This is a sacrifice — you are deliberately going to the mat to create the throw.

steps.title: Extend your body and arm as a block
steps.text: As you fall, extend your leg and/or arm along the mat at uke's shin level to create the barrier. Your extended position across uke's path is the structural element of the throw.

steps.title: Pull uke's arm to complete the sideways topple
steps.text: With your sleeve grip, pull uke's arm laterally and downward as you fall. Uke's forward momentum is redirected sideways over your blocking limb, and they fall beside you.

principles: Yoko-Otoshi is a side throw — the drop is perpendicular to uke's forward movement, not behind them (which would be Tani-Otoshi).
The throw requires forward momentum in uke. Against a static uke, the side drop is easily avoided by stepping.
The blocking element is at shin or ankle level — the barrier is low and intercepts forward movement of the legs.
This is a sutemi (sacrifice) throw — tori must commit fully to the drop. A hesitant, half-committed fall fails to create the blocking barrier.
The arm pull direction is the same as the fall direction — lateral and forward, not straight backward.

mistakes.mistake: Dropping directly behind uke instead of to the side
mistakes.fix: Yoko-Otoshi falls to the side (perpendicular). Falling directly behind creates Tani-Otoshi mechanics. Position your body perpendicular to uke's line of travel.

mistakes.mistake: Attempting on a static, non-moving uke
mistakes.fix: Create forward movement with your grips before dropping. Without uke's forward momentum, they simply step over the blocking leg.

mistakes.mistake: Block leg too high — uke steps over it
mistakes.fix: The blocking barrier should be at shin or ankle level. A thigh-level block is too high and can be stepped over.

mistakes.mistake: Half-hearted sacrifice — falling slowly and failing to create the barrier
mistakes.fix: Commit to the drop fully. Yoko-Otoshi must be a decisive lateral fall to create an effective blocking position.

when_to_use: Yoko-Otoshi is most effective when uke is stepping aggressively forward — during an attack entry, after a failed grip fight, or when uke is charging into you. The throw works as a counter to powerful forward pressure. It can also be applied as a sacrifice option when uke's guard is very tight from above but their forward step exposes the shin level.

faq.q: What is the difference between Yoko-Otoshi and Tani-Otoshi?
faq.a: Both are side sacrifice throws. Tani-Otoshi (valley drop) drops directly behind uke and sweeps their legs forward — the throw direction is backward. Yoko-Otoshi drops to the side (perpendicular to uke) and blocks uke's forward movement with a lateral barrier — the throw direction is sideways. The drop angle is the defining difference.

faq.q: Is Yoko-Otoshi in the Gokyo no Waza?
faq.a: Yes — Yoko-Otoshi is one of the classical techniques of the Gokyo no Waza, the five-group system of Kodokan judo techniques originally formalized in 1895.

faq.q: What belt level is Yoko-Otoshi?
faq.a: Yoko-Otoshi is typically introduced at 4th kyu (orange belt) or 3rd kyu (green belt) as part of the progression through the Gokyo no Waza.

faq.q: Why is Yoko-Otoshi called a sacrifice throw?
faq.a: In a sacrifice throw (sutemi-waza), tori deliberately falls to the mat as part of the throwing mechanism. Yoko-Otoshi requires tori to drop to the side, sacrificing their own standing position to create the barrier that topples uke.

name: Yoko-Shiho-Gatame
overview: Yoko-Shiho-Gatame is the most common hold-down used in competition judo. Tori controls uke from the side, pinning both their shoulders to the mat. One arm traps between uke's legs gripping their belt or trousers, the other controls uke's near arm and neck. The four-point contact of hands gives stable, rotational control.

videos.title: Escape Any Yoko Shiho Gatame - Travis Stevens Basic Judo Techniques

steps.title: Position at uke's right side, perpendicular to their body
steps.text: Kneel at uke's right side with your chest facing toward their feet. You are perpendicular to uke, facing toward their legs.

steps.title: Thread your left arm between uke's legs
steps.text: Slide your left arm between uke's legs and grip their belt, trouser hem, or the mat. This controls uke's lower body and prevents the bridge escape.

steps.title: Wrap your right arm around uke's neck/head
steps.text: Wrap your right arm under uke's neck, reaching to control their head, or trap uke's near arm under your armpit. The head control version is stronger for preventing uke's rotation. Grip their far collar or lapel.

steps.title: Drive your chest onto uke's chest
steps.text: Lower your chest down onto uke's sternum, applying body weight directly. Spread your knees wide for a stable base.

steps.title: Maintain position and adjust to uke's escape attempts
steps.text: Keep your weight on uke's chest. If uke turns into you, flow to Kami-Shiho-Gatame or mount. If they turn away, switch to the other side.

principles: The arm between the legs prevents the hip bridge escape — this is the critical control point.
Chest-to-chest contact: your body weight on uke's chest pins them.
Wide knee base: spread your knees to lower your center of gravity.
Follow uke's movement — if they roll, you roll with them rather than fighting their motion.

mistakes.mistake: Not threading the arm between the legs
mistakes.fix: This arm is essential for holding the lower body. Without it, uke bridges and rolls you off.

mistakes.mistake: Kneeling rather than spreading the legs wide
mistakes.fix: Spread your knees wide on the mat. A high kneeling position is easily rolled.

mistakes.mistake: Holding too rigidly — fighting uke's roll
mistakes.fix: If uke rolls one way, flow to a different pin. Fighting directly against rotation is tiring and unsuccessful.

mistakes.mistake: Placing a knee or hip on top of uke
mistakes.fix: In competition, kneeling or sitting on uke is prohibited (interpreted as kakaekomi). Keep your knees on the mat and your weight distributed through your chest and arms, not on top of uke's body.

when_to_use: Yoko-Shiho-Gatame transitions naturally from throws where uke lands on their back and tori is at their side. It is the most versatile hold-down for transitioning to pins on either side. From Yoko-Shiho-Gatame, tori can easily transition to mount, Kami-Shiho-Gatame, or arm locks.

faq.q: What is the scoring time for Yoko-Shiho-Gatame in competition?
faq.a: 20 seconds for ippon, 10-19 seconds for waza-ari under IJF rules.

faq.q: What belt level is Yoko-Shiho-Gatame taught at?
faq.a: Typically at 5th kyu (yellow belt) or 4th kyu (orange belt).

faq.q: What can be attacked from Yoko-Shiho-Gatame?
faq.a: Juji-Gatame (straight armlock) on the near arm, Ude-Garami (Kimura lock), and transitions to mount are all accessible from this position.

name: Yoko-Wakare
overview: Yoko-Wakare is a side sacrifice throw where tori falls to the side perpendicular to uke, using the fall and arm pull to sweep uke over and separate (wakare) from them as uke is thrown. It is one of the classical side sacrifice throws appearing in the Nage-no-Kata and illustrates the principle of using body weight and momentum from a side fall to achieve a throw.

videos.title: Yoko Wakare is highly effective when your opponent is not expecting it.

kuzushi.label: Off-balance
kuzushi.text: Pull uke strongly to the side — in the direction tori will fall. The sleeve and lapel grips pull uke's upper body toward tori's falling side. Uke's balance is broken sideways onto their front corner in the direction of the sacrifice.

tsukuri.label: Entry
tsukuri.text: Step across in front of uke and position your body perpendicular to uke's direction. As you begin to fall to the side, your body slides across uke's path. The sleeve grip maintains contact to guide uke's arm as you fall.

kake.label: Execution
kake.text: Fall directly to the side — the sacrifice. As you fall, pull uke's upper body over and in the direction of your fall using the grips. Your falling body weight and the arm pull together sweep uke over and separate you both — uke lands on the mat while tori is on their side.

steps.title: Create sideward kuzushi
steps.text: Pull uke toward your intended falling side with both grips. Uke's balance shifts sideways.

steps.title: Step across uke's path
steps.text: Step or swing your body across uke's front, perpendicular to them.

steps.title: Fall to the side — the sacrifice
steps.text: Fall directly to the side, committing fully. The fall must be decisive and take you fully to the ground.

steps.title: Pull uke with both grips
steps.text: As you fall, pull uke's upper body with the grips, directing them over and in the same direction as your fall.

steps.title: Separate from uke as they land
steps.text: Uke is thrown over and to the mat. The "wakare" (separation) occurs as your bodies separate at the landing — tori rolls clear.

principles: The fall must be complete and committed. A half-hearted fall leaves you partially upright and the throw incomplete.
The grips pull uke in the same direction as tori's fall. Both forces work together.
Yoko-Wakare is a classical technique — focus on clean execution and the principle of side sacrifice.
The "separation" (wakare) is built into the technique — tori and uke separate cleanly as the throw is completed.

mistakes.mistake: Falling too far behind uke — no directional leverage
mistakes.fix: Position your body perpendicular to uke before falling. The side fall must sweep across uke's path, not behind them.

mistakes.mistake: Not committing fully to the fall
mistakes.fix: Yoko-Wakare requires total sacrifice. A partial fall results in a tangled position, not a clean throw.

mistakes.mistake: Losing grip during the fall
mistakes.fix: Maintain grips throughout the fall. The grips direct uke's trajectory and prevent them from simply stepping over tori.

mistakes.mistake: Insufficient kuzushi before falling
mistakes.fix: Pull uke off balance before sacrificing. Falling when uke is upright and balanced means they simply step over you.

when_to_use: Yoko-Wakare is most practical when uke is moving to the side or when the position of uke relative to tori makes a side sacrifice more accessible than a forward throw. It is a Nage-no-Kata technique and is regularly practiced in kata training.

faq.q: Is Yoko-Wakare commonly used in shiai?
faq.a: Yoko-Wakare is seen more in kata training than in competition. In shiai, side sacrifice throws require precise timing and commitment that makes them higher-risk. More dynamic side sacrifice variants like Yoko-Gake are seen more often in competition.

faq.q: What does "wakare" mean?
faq.a: "Wakare" means separation or parting. In Yoko-Wakare, the bodies of tori and uke separate cleanly as the throw is completed — tori falls to the side while uke is swept over them.
